calcom-10600.issue: Accessibility regression: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the password visibility toggle button removes it from keyboard tab order. Keyboard-only users can no longer toggle password visibility, which is an accessibility regression for a shared UI component used by all password fields (including the login and 2FA password inputs in this PR). If the intent was to prevent the toggle from stealing focus during form autofill/submission, a more targeted fix (e.g., `onMouseDown={e => e.preventDefault()}`) would preserve keyboard access.

Input validation gap: The `minLength={10}` / `maxLength={11}` constraints don't enforce the expected format. A 10-character value containing a dash (e.g. "1234-56789") passes HTML validation, but the server strips dashes before comparing (`replaceAll("-", "")`), so it becomes a 9-character string that can never match a stored 10-character code. Similarly, arbitrary non-code characters are accepted since there is no `pattern` check. Adding a pattern like `^[0-9a-f]{5}-?[0-9a-f]{5}$` (matching the hex codes generated server-side) would reject malformed input up front instead of producing a confusing "incorrect backup code" error.

Missing validation feedback: The field is marked `required` but no error message or `aria-invalid` handling is provided, and unlike the sibling `TwoFactor` component (which gained an `autoFocus` prop in this PR), this component offers no `autoFocus` option. When the user submits the login/disable forms with an empty backup code, browser-native validation text appears with no styled feedback consistent with the rest of the form, and keyboard users landing on the backup-code step must manually tab to the field.

Conflicting defaultValue: `defaultValue=""` is passed alongside `{...methods.register("backupCode")}`. In react-hook-form, the registered input's value is controlled by the form state; the explicit `defaultValue` prop is redundant and can conflict with `methods.setValue("backupCode", "")` reset calls made by the parent forms (login.tsx and DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx), depending on render timing. Dropping `defaultValue` (or using `defaultValues` in `useForm`) is the conventional pattern.

Backup codes silently invalidated: Every call to the setup endpoint overwrites `backupCodes` with a freshly generated set. If a user who already has 2FA enabled (and previously saved backup codes) opens the setup flow again — or calls it repeatedly without completing enablement — their previously issued backup codes are destroyed and replaced, even if the user cancels the setup afterwards. A user relying on a saved backup code will find it rejected at login. Consider only generating backup codes when they don't already exist, or confirming before regenerating.

Unhandled JSON.parse: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...))` is called without a try/catch. If the stored `backupCodes` value is corrupted, was written by an older format, or decryption yields non-JSON output, this throws an unhandled exception and the client receives a raw 500 instead of a structured error. The sibling login flow in `next-auth-options.ts` has the same pattern, but here the failure also aborts the disable flow entirely. Wrap the parse/decrypt in try/catch and return a 400/500 JSON error.

Unvalidated input type: `req.body.backupCode` is used directly in `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` without validating it is a string. A client posting `{"backupCode": 123}` or `{"backupCode": {"a": 1}}` (JSON bodies allow non-string values) causes `replaceAll` to throw a TypeError, resulting in an unhandled 500 rather than the intended `IncorrectBackupCode` 400 response. Add a `typeof req.body.backupCode === "string"` check.

Untested assertion: The newly added FIXME documents that the existing `isChecked()` check on `two-factor-switch` passes even when the switch is not checked, yet the assertion is left in place and the underlying bug is not fixed in this PR. Since this helper is used to set up every 2FA test in the file, a regression that leaves 2FA disabled after setup could go undetected while later steps fail with confusing errors. Consider replacing it with the reliable `data-state="checked"` visibility check already used a few lines below.

Missing assertions: The new backup-code steps include TODOs for verifying the downloaded file content and the clipboard content, so the test only asserts that a download named `cal-backup-codes.txt` occurs and that a success toast appears. A regression that downloads empty or wrong backup codes (e.g., a formatting bug in `formatBackupCode`) would pass this test. At minimum, reading the download stream and asserting it contains 10 codes in `XXXXX-XXXXX` format would close the gap.

Unhandled JSON.parse: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, ...))` is called without a try/catch. If the stored `backupCodes` value is corrupted, was encrypted with a different/rotated `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, or is otherwise not valid JSON, `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` will throw an unhandled exception inside `authorize`. This surfaces as an opaque NextAuth internal error instead of a user-facing message, and unlike the other failure paths (IncorrectBackupCode, MissingBackupCodes) the login page cannot map it to a helpful error. Wrapping the decrypt/parse in a try/catch and throwing `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes` (or a dedicated error) would degrade gracefully.

Backup code consumed on match only after password check - but no rate-limit distinction: The backup-code verification uses `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` (a plain string comparison) on secrets that are long-lived, reusable-until-used credentials. Unlike TOTP codes (30-second window), a backup code remains valid indefinitely, so an attacker who can repeatedly hit `authorize` with a password candidate can brute-force the 40-bit code space without any per-code expiry. If the existing rate limit earlier in `authorize` applies per-email/password and is not tightened for failed backup-code attempts, this is a weaker link than the TOTP path. Note: I cannot see the full rate-limiting configuration in this diff, so the actual exposure depends on limits defined elsewhere.

Possible Bug: The login form uses `zodResolver(formSchema)` and `LoginValues` now includes `backupCode`, but the new backup-code flow is not reflected in the form validation shown/updated in this diff. If `formSchema` still requires `totpCode` (as the previous flow did), submitting the form while `twoFactorLostAccess` is true — with an empty `totpCode` — would fail client-side validation before ever reaching the server, making the "lost access" backup-code path unusable. Conversely, if `backupCode` was added to the schema as required, the normal TOTP path would fail. Verify the schema allows exactly one of the two fields depending on the active mode. (Uncertain because `formSchema` is not shown in the diff, but it is defined in this file and was not updated here.)

Stale State: When the server responds with `ErrorCode.SecondFactorRequired`, only `twoFactorRequired` is set to true; `twoFactorLostAccess` is never reset. If a user toggled "lost access", submitted a wrong backup code, then went all the way back and re-submitted credentials triggering 2FA again, the stale `twoFactorLostAccess` state could leave the form showing the backup-code input (or an inconsistent footer) instead of the TOTP input. Resetting `twoFactorLostAccess` alongside `setTwoFactorRequired(true)` would make the state deterministic.

Stale validation errors: `resetForm` clears field values via `form.setValue` and the error message state, but does not call `form.clearErrors()` or `form.reset()`. Since the `PasswordField` is now marked `required` and `BackupCode` registers a `required` field, a failed HTML/react-hook-form validation leaves error state attached to fields; after toggling between "Lost access" and TOTP modes (which calls `resetForm(false)`), the user can be shown stale validation errors for a field that is no longer visible, blocking submission with no visible cause. Low severity, but easy to fix by clearing errors in `resetForm`.

Submit not guarded in lost-access toggle: The "Lost access"/"Go back" footer button remains enabled while `isDisabling` is true (the submit button is disabled via `isDisabling`, but this toggle is not). Clicking it mid-request switches the input mode and calls `resetForm`, clearing `backupCode`/`totpCode` values while the disable request is in flight, which can produce a confusing success/error state on return. Minor UX inconsistency rather than a data-integrity bug.

Possible Bug: The download button inside the backup-codes step is a `Button` with no explicit `type`, rendered inside the `<Form handleSubmit={handleEnable}>`. Unlike the copy and close buttons (which call `e.preventDefault()`), clicking the download anchor will also submit the surrounding form, invoking `handleEnable` with an empty/missing `totpCode` and surfacing a validation/error state while the user is only trying to download the codes. Give the button `type="button"` (or move the backup-codes footer outside the form).

State inconsistency on dialog close: At the `DisplayBackupCodes` step the cancel button is hidden and the only in-dialog exit is the "close" button, which calls `resetState()` and `onEnable()`. However, closing the dialog via the backdrop, ESC key, or `onOpenChange` (handled by the parent through the `Dialog`'s `onOpenChange`) bypasses both: `onEnable()` is never called (so the parent never learns 2FA was enabled) and `resetState()` never runs, leaving stale step/backup-codes state if the modal is reopened. A user who dismisses the dialog this way also never sees the backup codes, which cannot be recovered later.

Incomplete state reset: `resetState()` clears the password, error, and step but not `backupCodes` or `backupCodesUrl`. The generated backup codes and their blob URL persist in component state after the flow completes. Since the modal is mounted per-open this is low severity, but if the component is reused the stale secret material lingers in memory and the object URL is never revoked on unmount.

calcom-10967.issue: Missing fallback: The new array-wrapping logic matches the sibling handlers (confirm.handler.ts, editLocation.handler.ts, handleCancelBooking.ts), which all fall back to the user's destinationCalendar when the booking has none: `booking?.destinationCalendar ? [booking.destinationCalendar] : booking?.user?.destinationCalendar ? [...] : []`. Here there is no fallback to `bookingToReschedule?.user?.destinationCalendar` (or the eventType's calendar), so for bookings without their own destinationCalendar the reschedule event will always get an empty array. Note the pre-PR code also lacked this fallback (it was a redundant self-OR), so this is not a regression introduced by the PR, but it is an inconsistency with the convention established in the other changed files that may cause the rescheduled event to be created on the wrong calendar. Worth confirming whether the fallback is intentionally omitted here.

Possible Bug: The refactor of the `slug` spread inverts the original condition. Previously the code spread `slug` into the organization create payload when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` was false (`...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`). The new code spreads `slug` only when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` is true (`...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`). When team billing is enabled, the organization will now be created with a `slug` where it previously was not (and vice versa), changing which organizations get a slug persisted at creation. If the intent was only to make the conditional spread explicit, the condition should remain negated: `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`. Note the adjacent `requestedSlug` line keeps the original condition (`IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED`), which suggests the `slug` line's inversion is unintentional.

Wrong calendar selection for multi-host: `createEvent` always uses `destinationCalendar[0]` (the "main host" calendar) to build the events URL. Unlike the Google Calendar service in this same PR, which selects the destination matching the passed `credentialId`, this service has no way to know which credential it is being invoked for. With the new collective-event flow in `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents`, `createEvent` is called once per destination calendar with that host's credential. When the Office365 credential belongs to a non-first host, the event will still be created in the first host's calendar (or `/me/calendar/events` if that entry has no externalId), i.e. in the wrong user's calendar. Consider accepting the `credentialId` parameter (per the updated `Calendar` interface) and finding the matching destination by `credentialId`, as the Google implementation does.

Wrong calendar selected for collective events: All four methods now blindly use the first element of `event.destinationCalendar` (`mainHostDestinationCalendar`). For COLLECTIVE team events, `handleNewBooking.ts` pushes every member's destination calendar into the array, so the first entry may belong to a different host (e.g., a Google Calendar), while this Lark service instance is operating with a specific Lark credential. The Google service in this same PR resolves the correct calendar by matching `credentialId` (createEvent now receives `credentialId` per the updated `Calendar` interface), but `LarkCalendarService.createEvent` was not updated to accept `credentialId` and does no credential/`integration` matching. In a collective booking where the organizer uses Google and a team member uses Lark, the Lark service would attempt to create/update/delete the event on the first (Google) calendar's `externalId`, causing failures or events landing on the wrong calendar. Consider matching the destination calendar by credentialId or integration type, as the Google service does.

Stale reference on failure: The new `externalId` and `credentialId` fields are returned unconditionally in the result object, even when event creation failed (`success: false`, e.g. the 404 catch path or any error where `creationResult` is `undefined`). Downstream, `EventManager.createEventViaCalendar` builds booking references using `externalCalendarId: result.externalId` and `credentialId: result.credentialId` without checking `result.success`, so a booking reference can be persisted pointing to a calendar event that was never created. On a later reschedule/update or cancellation, `updateEventForBooking`/delete logic will then attempt to operate on (or trust) a nonexistent external event. Consider only populating `externalId`/`credentialId` when `success` is true, or having the caller skip failed results when building references.

Missing externalId in fallback path: `externalId` is only forwarded when the caller passes it (the per-destination loop in `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` with a `credentialId`). In the fallback branch where a destination has no `credentialId`, `createEvent(c, event)` is called without `externalId`, so the returned result has `externalId: undefined` while `credentialId` is now set. Callers that previously derived `externalCalendarId` from `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` (the old EventManager behavior) will now record `undefined` for these bookings, changing what gets stored in booking references for that path. Verify this is intentional for the no-credentialId case.

Possible Bug: In `updateEvent`, the fallback now does `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. When `externalCalendarId` is undefined (the common case for bookings without an explicit external calendar id), the predicate compares `cal.externalId === undefined` and never matches, so `selectedCalendar` is undefined and `calendar.events.update` is called with an undefined `calendarId`, which will fail. The old code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` in this case. The fallback should probably match on something else (e.g. return the first/main host calendar) when `externalCalendarId` is not provided.

Possible Bug: Same pattern in `deleteEvent`: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` never matches when `externalCalendarId` is undefined, so `calendarId` becomes undefined and the delete call targets an undefined calendar id. Previously it fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`, so deletions that worked before will now fail for bookings without an `externalCalendarId` reference.

Silent fallback: In `createEvent`, `selectedCalendar` is resolved by matching `cal.credentialId === credentialId`, and if no destination calendar matches, the event is silently created on `"primary"`. Previously the event was created on `destinationCalendar.externalId`. If a collective booking's destination calendar entry has a credentialId that doesn't match this credential (e.g. stale or mismatched data), the event now lands on the user's primary calendar with no warning, which may be hard to notice and clean up. Consider logging or surfacing a warning when falling back to "primary".

Duplicate deletions: The recurring-event deletion block now runs once per calendar reference (the outer `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop), but inside it iterates over all of the user's calendar credentials and all `updatedBookings`, deleting each booking's first calendar-reference event. With multiple calendar references (the very scenario this PR enables for collective events), the same set of calendar events will be deleted N times — once per reference. The outer `reference` variable is not even used inside this branch, so the extra iterations add no new deletions, only repeated `deleteEvent` calls against the same events. This should be hoisted out of the per-reference loop (or the branch should use the current `reference`'s credential/uid).

Only first reference used: Inside the recurring branch, `updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))` still picks only the first calendar reference per booking. Since this PR's purpose is to support multiple calendar references per booking (collective events with multiple hosts), any additional calendar references on the updated bookings are ignored and their events are never deleted, leaving orphaned calendar events for the other hosts.

Possible Bug: `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither `eventType.destinationCalendar` nor `organizerUser.destinationCalendar` exists. The subsequent `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op on `null`, so for a COLLECTIVE team event where the organizer/event type have no destination calendar, all team members' destination calendars are silently dropped and no calendar event is created for them. The push should be guarded to initialize the array (e.g., `evt.destinationCalendar = [...(evt.destinationCalendar ?? []), ...teamDestinationCalendars]`).

Data Loss: The booking creation now connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]` to the booking record. For COLLECTIVE team events, `evt.destinationCalendar` may contain multiple calendars (organizer plus team members pushed via `teamDestinationCalendars`), but only the first one is persisted via `connect`. The remaining calendars are never linked to the booking, so subsequent reschedule/cancel flows that read `booking.destinationCalendar` will not see the other members' calendars. If persisting all of them is intended, this should be `connect: evt.destinationCalendar.map((cal) => ({ id: cal.id }))`.

Possible Bug: `evt.destinationCalendar` is now an array (or null/empty). The destructuring `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` when the array is empty or null, and the next line accesses `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. This throws a TypeError for any booking where no destination calendar is set (e.g., users with no calendar connected), crashing event creation. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration` and handled this safely.

Undefined credential passed to updateEvent: In `updateAllCalendarEvents`, when a reference has a `credentialId` that is not found in `this.calendarCredentials`, the code fetches it from the DB, but only assigns it if `credentialFromDB.app?.slug` is truthy. If the credential exists but has no associated app (or the DB lookup returns null, e.g., credential deleted), `credential` remains `undefined` and `updateEvent(credential, ...)` is still called, likely throwing inside the calendar service instead of being skipped or reported. The same pattern exists in `createAllCalendarEvents`, though there the `if (credential)` guard prevents the call.

Lost externalCalendarId: In the second result-mapping block (~line 205), `externalCalendarId` is now taken from `result.externalId`. But in `createAllCalendarEvents`, the no-credentialId branch calls `createEvent(c, event)` without passing `destination.externalId`, so `result.externalId` is `undefined` for events created via that path. Previously `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId` was used directly, so the booking reference's `externalCalendarId` is now lost for bookings whose destination calendar has no credentialId, which can break later update/delete of those calendar events.

calcom-22345.issue: Test coverage removed: The "Caching" describe block was deleted entirely, but the service still caches authorization and filter conditions (`cachedAuthConditions` / `cachedFilterConditions` in insightsBooking.ts). With these tests gone, a regression that breaks caching (e.g., conditions rebuilt on every call, or a stale cache returned after options change) would no longer be caught. If the caching behavior is intentionally no longer tested, the caching logic itself should arguably also be removed; otherwise the tests should be ported to the new `Prisma.Sql` representation.

Possible Bug: `Prisma.sql` expands a JS array parameter into a comma-separated list of bind placeholders (it is designed for `IN (${ids})` usage). Wrapping it as `ANY(${teamIds})` therefore produces `ANY($1, $2, ...)` which is invalid PostgreSQL syntax and will throw at query time. The same applies to `ANY(${uniqueUserIds})` and `ANY(${userIdsFromTeam})`. Use `IN (...)` instead, or construct a proper array (e.g. `ANY(${Prisma.join(teamIds)}::int[])` / `ARRAY[...]`).

Possible Bug: In `buildOrgAuthorizationCondition`, if `teamIds` is empty (organization with no child teams), the generated fragment becomes `("teamId" = ANY()) AND ...` which is a SQL syntax error. The old Prisma `in: []` condition safely evaluated to false. Guard the empty-array case (e.g. return `NOTHING_CONDITION` or skip the condition) before emitting the `ANY` clause.

Type inconsistency: The constructor now accepts `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`, where `teamId` is optional, but `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` still types its parameter via `Extract<InsightsBookingServiceOptions, { scope: "team" }>`, which requires `teamId`. At runtime a caller can pass `{ scope: "team", userId, orgId }` without `teamId`, and `options.teamId` will be `undefined` when passed to `findByIdAndParentId` and interpolated into the SQL fragment. Either make `teamId` required for the team scope in the public type or validate it before use.

calcom-22532.issue: Possible Bug: `updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` is called with an empty `data` object. Prisma's `updateMany` with an empty data payload can raise a validation error, and even if accepted, it relies entirely on Prisma's `@updatedAt` side effect to bump `updatedAt` — the comment says the intent is to update `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`, but no field is actually passed. If `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is not annotated with `@updatedAt` (this PR only adds that annotation to `CalendarCache`), the call updates nothing and the cache-status feature silently shows stale data. Passing an explicit field (e.g. a last-synced timestamp) would make the intent robust.

Unconditional write on read path: The update runs on every invocation of this method, touching all `SelectedCalendar` rows for the credential even when the availability fetch was served from a fresh cache or only one calendar's data changed. This adds a DB write per availability check (a hot path during booking flows) and makes `updatedAt` reflect "any fetch happened" rather than a meaningful per-calendar sync time, weakening the cache-status signal this PR introduces.

Dependency resolution: The `dev:cron` script now uses `npx tsx` instead of a package-manager-managed binary. If `tsx` is not declared as a devDependency of this workspace, `npx` will silently download and run it from the npm registry at invocation time, pinning no version and making the dev script depend on network access and whatever the latest `tsx` release is. Prefer adding `tsx` to devDependencies and invoking it directly (e.g., `yarn tsx cron-tester.ts`) so the version is locked and no implicit fetch occurs.

Expired cache reported as valid: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups `CalendarCache` rows by `credentialId` and returns only the max `updatedAt`, without filtering on `expiresAt`. Cache entries in this table carry an `expiresAt` field (visible in the schema), so a credential whose only cache rows are already expired will still be reported as having a valid cache with a recent `updatedAt`. The UI (CredentialActionsDropdown) uses this value to display "Cache Status / Last updated", so users will see a healthy cache status for credentials whose cached availability has actually expired. Consider adding `expiresAt: { gt: new Date() }` to the `where` clause, or returning expiry info so callers can decide.

Possible Bug: `updateManyByCredentialId` is called from `CalendarService.ts` with an empty data object (`{}`). Prisma's `updateMany` throws a `PrismaClientValidationError` when `data` contains no fields to update, so every availability refresh for a Google credential would fail at this call. Even if Prisma accepted it, an empty update would not bump any timestamp, so the intended "touch updatedAt" behavior (used to surface cache status in the UI) would not happen. The method should either explicitly set the field it intends to bump (e.g., `updatedAt: new Date()`) or the caller should pass meaningful data.

Unconditional extra DB query: The handler now runs a `calendarCache.groupBy` query on every `connectedCalendars` fetch, regardless of whether the calendar-cache feature is enabled or whether any of the credentials actually use caching (e.g., non-Google calendar credentials will always be queried too). Since `connectedCalendars` is a frequently called tRPC query (also invalidated/refetched after mutations in the UI), this adds a database round-trip to a hot path. Consider gating the query behind the calendar-cache feature flag (the repository already has a disabled/mock variant, but the real repository performs the query unconditionally) or filtering `credentialIds` to cache-enabled integration types before calling `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`.

Portability Bug: `sed -i '' -E ...` is macOS/BSD-specific syntax. On GNU/Linux, `sed -i ''` treats the empty string as the script argument (empty script), causing sed to error out and the existing `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=` line in the env file to never be updated. On a Linux dev environment where the env file already contains the key, the script prints the success message but the value is silently not replaced.

Stale tunnel URL: When Tunnelmole is already running, the URL is extracted from the pre-existing log file, which may be from a previous session with a different (now-dead) tunnel URL, or the log file may not exist at all (grep on a missing file fails silently). In the latter case the script prints "Failed to extract Tunnelmole URL" and exits, even though a valid tmole process is running and could have been queried differently. The webhook URL written to the env file may therefore point at a stale tunnel.

Misleading exit code: `cleanup` always calls `exit 0`, including on the failure paths (rate limit hit, failed URL extraction). Callers of this script (e.g., CI or a wrapping npm script) cannot detect that the setup failed and will proceed as if the tunnel was established.

Hardcoded locale: The cache timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, hardcoding the US locale regardless of the user's actual locale. A user with a non-English locale will see dates formatted in US style (e.g., "7/15/25, 4:06 PM") while the rest of the UI is localized. Use the locale from `useLocale()` (or `navigator.language`) instead.

Stale cache status: After `deleteCacheMutation` succeeds, the component only calls `onSuccess?.()` and shows a toast, but unlike `disconnectMutation` (which explicitly invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`), it does not invalidate that query itself. If the parent's `onSuccess` callback does not trigger a refetch of `connectedCalendars`, the dropdown will keep showing the old "Last updated" timestamp and the "Delete cached data" option even though the cache rows are gone. Consider mirroring the invalidation done in `disconnectMutation.onSettled` for consistency.

calcom-8087.issue: Possible Bug: With the appStore now holding dynamic `import()` promises, `await appStore[...]` will throw if the module fails to load (e.g., a broken build chunk, network/CDN error at runtime in a serverless environment). Previously a missing/failed app simply resulted in `undefined`, which the following guard handled gracefully by logging a warning and returning `null`. Now the rejection propagates and can fail the whole payment-handling flow with an unhandled error instead of the intended graceful degradation. Consider wrapping the await in a try/catch (or `Promise.resolve(...).catch(() => undefined)`) to preserve the old behavior.

Unawaited async forEach: Changing the `forEach` callback to `async` means the promises returned by the callbacks (including `await getCalendar(...)` and `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)`) are not awaited by anyone. `Array.prototype.forEach` ignores return values, so `Reschedule` can complete (and the surrounding `try` block exits) before any calendar event deletion actually runs, and any rejection from `deleteEvent` or `getCalendar` becomes an unhandled promise rejection that the `try/catch` cannot catch. If a calendar deletion fails, the caller will never know. Using `for...of` with `await`, or `Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`, would preserve error handling and completion guarantees.

Unawaited async forEach: Changing the `forEach` callback to `async` makes the callback return a Promise that is ignored: `forEach` does not await promises. As a result, the `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` and `deleteMeeting(...)` calls become fire-and-forget — the enclosing `try/catch` no longer catches any errors from them (rejections become unhandled promise rejections), and callers of `Reschedule` cannot know whether calendar/video events were actually deleted. If the intent is sequential awaited deletion, use a `for...of` loop; if parallel, collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)` inside the try block.

Fire-and-forget async forEach: Changing the `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` callback to `async` makes each callback return a promise that `forEach` discards. The calendar `deleteEvent` calls are no longer tracked: the surrounding reschedule logic (and its `try`/error handling, if any) completes before deletions finish, and any rejection from `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent` becomes an unhandled promise rejection with no logging or propagation. A realistic trigger: a calendar credential whose dynamic import fails or whose `deleteEvent` throws — the deletion silently fails while the booking is rescheduled as if it succeeded. Use a `for...of` loop with `await` (as done elsewhere in this PR, e.g. in `handleCancelBooking.ts`) or collect promises with `Promise.all`.

No lazy-loading benefit: Each `import("./...")` call is executed eagerly at module load time, so every app package is still fetched and evaluated when `packages/app-store/index.ts` is first imported. Dynamic `import()` only defers work when the call itself is deferred (e.g., inside a function keyed by app name). As written, this converts the static imports into promise-valued properties without actually reducing startup work or bundle loading; if the goal of the PR is lazy/async loading, the imports should be wrapped in a factory (e.g., `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) or resolved on demand.

Fire-and-forget async forEach: The `.forEach(async (credential) => { ... })` block now awaits `getCalendar(credential)` (and subsequently the per-booking delete/update calls) inside an async forEach callback. forEach does not wait for the returned promises, so these deletions run detached from the handler: the function can complete (and the response be returned) before the calendar events are deleted, and any rejection from the dynamic import inside `getCalendar` or from `deleteEvent` becomes an unhandled promise rejection with no logging or surfacing to the caller. Since `getCalendar` is now async (it awaits a dynamic import that can reject), this pre-existing fire-and-forget pattern can now fail silently in a new way. Consider `for...of` with await, or `Promise.all(credentials.map(...))` with error handling.

Sequential awaits in loop: The refactored loop awaits `getCalendar(credential)` sequentially for each calendar credential. Since each `getCalendar` call now resolves a dynamic module import, these are independent and could be run concurrently with `Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map(...))`, avoiding serializing module loads on the cancellation path. Low severity, but a straightforward improvement in the exact code being touched.

grafana-103633.issue: This new code guards two different cache lookups ('permDenialCache' and 'getCachedIdentityPermissions') before making a decision, but they don't get the same trust: 'permDenialCache' returns immediately on a cache hit, while 'getCachedIdentityPermissions''s hit branches internally and doesn't return for at least one of its outcomes.
grafana-103633.suggestion: Confirm this asymmetry is intentional; if not, make both branches return immediately on a hit (or neither does) so a cached result isn't trusted differently depending on which outcome it represents.

grafana-103633.issue: Cache key collision: `userPermDenialCacheKey` builds the key by naive string concatenation with "_" separators and no escaping. Since user UIDs, actions, resource names, and folder names are arbitrary strings that may themselves contain "_", two different (userUID, action, name, parent) tuples can produce the same key — e.g. user "u_1"/action "read"/name "x"/parent "" vs user "u"/action "1_read"/name "x"/parent "" — causing a denial cached for one request to wrongly deny a different request. A denial is a security-relevant cached value, so a delimiter that cannot appear in the components (or explicit escaping) would be safer.

Test coverage gap: The new `TestService_CacheList` only covers the cache-hit path for `List`. Unlike `TestService_CacheCheck`, which covers cache miss, outdated cache, and explicit denial, there are no tests for `List` falling back to the database on a cache miss or for how `List` interacts with `permDenialCache`. Since `List` was changed to use `getCachedIdentityPermissions` in this PR, these paths are currently untested.

Stale denial overrides fresh grant: The new `permDenialCache` is checked first in `Check` and short-circuits to a deny before the permission cache is consulted. Once a deny is cached (on any denied check), a subsequent grant of access to that resource (e.g., an admin adds a permission for the user) will still be denied for up to `shortCacheTTL`, because the denial entry is never invalidated by permission changes and it takes precedence over the (fresh) `permCache` allow path. A concrete scenario: user is denied `dashboards:read` on `dash1`, then granted the permission; every Check for `dash1` returns `Allowed: false` from the denial cache until the TTL expires, even though `permCache` may already reflect the new allow. Consider invalidating denial entries on permission updates, or checking the allow path before the denial cache.

Silent fallback on cache errors: In `Check`, `getCachedIdentityPermissions` errors are treated uniformly as a cache miss (`if err == nil`). A real error from `GetUserIdentifiers` (e.g., DB failure) is swallowed and the code falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which will repeat the same failing lookup and produce a second error/log. This doubles the failing DB work per request and hides the first error. Distinguishing `cache.ErrNotFound` from other errors (as the cache-miss semantics intend) would avoid the redundant work.

grafana-76186.issue: Contract violation: `TestLogger.FromContext` ignores both the receiver's state and the passed `context.Context`, returning a brand-new `NewTestLogger()`. The `Logger.FromContext` contract (per the interface comment in `pkg/plugins/log/ifaces.go` and the real implementation in `grafanaInfraLogWrapper`) is to return a logger carrying this logger's context plus the given context. A test helper using `TestLogger` will therefore silently lose any accumulated logs/context when code calls `FromContext`, making the fake diverge from real behavior and potentially masking bugs in tests that rely on it.

Silent context loss on fallback: In `FromContext`, if the type assertion to `*log.ConcreteLogger` fails, the method silently falls back to `d.New()`, which returns a logger with this wrapper's context but none of the attributes carried in the passed `context.Context`. The caller (e.g., `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` calling `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)`) expects contextual attributes from the context to appear in log output; on the fallback path they are silently dropped with no logging or error. If the assertion can realistically fail (e.g., the infra logger's `FromContext` returns a non-pointer or a different concrete type), contextual log fields would be lost intermittently. Consider logging a warning or verifying the assertion covers all return shapes of the infra logger.

Missing tests: This new middleware has no unit tests. The sibling `metrics_middleware_test.go` covers the metrics middleware, but nothing verifies that `instrumentContext` correctly attaches `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, and `uname` attributes to the context, nor that the middleware is wired into `CreateMiddlewares` in the intended order relative to `LoggerMiddleware` (which now depends on the contextual attributes being present in the context via `FromContext`).

Lost traceID in logs: The `traceID` field (previously added via `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)`) was removed from the "Plugin Request Completed" log parameters, and the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` (which now supplies pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID via contextual attributes) does not add a traceID either. As a result, plugin data-egress log lines can no longer be correlated with their distributed traces, a regression for debugging/observability workflows. If trace correlation is intended to be handled elsewhere (e.g., the tracing middleware injecting into the context), that path is not visible in this diff.

grafana-79265.issue: Type mismatch: The new `AnonymousDeviceLimit` field is populated unconditionally from `hs.Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit` (an int64 defaulting to 0), and the DTO serializes it without `omitempty`. The TypeScript counterpart added in this PR declares `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined`, so the `undefined` case can never actually occur — the frontend will always receive a number (0 even when anonymous access is disabled or no limit is set). Consider omitting the field when anonymous access is disabled or the limit is unset, or aligning the TS type with the actual always-present number to avoid frontend code branching on a state that never happens.

No upper bound on device_limit: `AnonymousDeviceLimit` is read with `MustInt64(0)` without validating a sensible range. A negative value (e.g. `device_limit = -5`) is treated as "no limit" by the store (`if s.deviceLimit > 0`), which silently disables the limit instead of either erroring or being rejected at startup. A typo'd or malicious config value can therefore silently change behavior. Consider validating the value (e.g., reject negatives) in `readAuthSettings`.

Performance regression: Device tagging was moved from a background goroutine (with its own 2-minute timeout and detached context) to a synchronous call on the request context inside `Authenticate`. Every anonymous request now blocks on the `TagDevice` DB work, which with the new device-limit path includes a `CountDevices` query plus an UPDATE/INSERT on every untagged request. Under anonymous traffic this adds DB latency to the hot authentication path, and if the request context is cancelled (client disconnects mid-request) the tagging is aborted, so devices may never be recorded. Consider keeping the tagging asynchronous or at least off the critical path.

Behavior change on errors: When `TagDevice` fails with `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, `Authenticate` now returns `nil, err`, so the anonymous user gets no identity and the request fails outright. This is presumably the intended enforcement of the limit, but note the side effect: once the limit is reached, all previously-unseen devices are completely locked out of the instance (not just untracked), and the raw internal error (`device limit reached`) is surfaced to the caller without mapping to a user-friendly/HTTP-appropriate error. Verify callers render this sensibly.

Behavior change in TagDevice: `TagDevice` previously swallowed errors from `tagDeviceUI` (logging at Debug level) and always returned nil, treating UI tagging as best-effort. It now returns the error. Any caller other than the `client.go` Authenticate path (which was updated in this PR to tolerate non-limit errors) that relied on `TagDevice` succeeding will now see failures for transient UI-tagging problems (e.g., DB errors), even when SSO tagging succeeded. If this propagation is intentional, the Debug-level log plus returned error is redundant/misleading (the error is surfaced, not just debug info); consider logging at Warn or documenting the new contract. Severity is moderate since the visible caller handles it, but the semantic change is easy to miss for other callers.

Race condition: The limit enforcement in `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is a non-atomic check-then-act: it counts devices with `CountDevices`, then inserts a new row if the count is below the limit. Under concurrent anonymous requests (the common case for a busy public instance), multiple goroutines can all observe `count < deviceLimit` and each insert, so the actual number of devices can exceed the configured limit. Since `TagDevice` is now called synchronously in the auth path (per client.go changes), concurrent logins are realistic. Consider enforcing the limit atomically (e.g., a transaction with a lock, or a conditional insert).

Error conflation: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `rowsAffected == 0`, but that outcome also occurs when the device row exists yet its stored `updated_at` falls outside the `[device.UpdatedAt - 30d, device.UpdatedAt + 1min]` window (e.g., a device not seen for over 30 days, or a caller passing a stale `UpdatedAt`). In that case the caller cannot distinguish "limit reached, new device rejected" from "existing device update silently failed", and downstream (client.go) `ErrDeviceLimitReached` aborts authentication. A returning device older than the expiration window will be permanently unable to re-tag while the limit is full, even if it is counted toward the limit and could legitimately replace itself. Consider distinguishing "device not found/stale" from "limit reached", or allowing an existing device to update its own row regardless of the window.

grafana-80329.issue: Performance concern: The cleanup job interval is reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute. Combined with the PR's new batched select-then-delete strategy in the annotations store, this means the cleanup queries (including full scans for orphaned annotation tags) run 10x more frequently against the database. If this frequency increase is intentional to compensate for the deadlock workaround, consider documenting it; otherwise the previous 10-minute interval may be more appropriate for production database load.

Wrong log level: Routine cleanup progress is logged with `r.log.Error` in all three cleanup paths (by time, by count, and orphaned tags), including a success message ("cleaned annotations by time", etc.). These are normal operations, not errors, and the cleanup job now runs every minute, so this will flood error logs/alerting pipelines on every deployment. Additionally, the `"err", err` key is logged when `err` is known to be nil at that point. These should be Debug/Info level, with error logging only on failure.

Unbounded log volume: The log statements include `"ids", ids`, dumping every fetched ID. With `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` configurable (the new test exercises 32767), a single batch can log tens of thousands of IDs, and this repeats every batch and every cleanup cycle. This can produce very large log lines and degrade logging infrastructure. Consider logging only the count, or capping the printed IDs.

Possible infinite loop: `untilDoneOrCancelled` relies on the batch returning zero affected rows to terminate. In the new flow, `fetchIDs` and `deleteByIDs` are separate statements; if rows are deleted concurrently between the SELECT and the DELETE, a batch can fetch non-empty IDs but affect 0 rows. If the concurrent deleter keeps pace, subsequent fetches can keep returning (different) rows while deletes keep affecting 0, causing the loop to spin until context cancellation rather than completing. Under the stated design ("may under-delete when concurrent inserts happen") this is plausible under heavy write load; consider also stopping when `len(ids) == 0` after a zero-affected batch, or bounding retries.

Fragile test data setup: `createTestAnnotations` now assigns explicit primary keys (`ID: int64(i + 1)`) and inserts them with `InsertMulti`, which assumes the `annotation` table is empty. The `t.Cleanup` that empties `annotation` and `annotation_tag` is registered inside each subtest only *after* `createTestAnnotations` and the initial count assertions run. If `createTestAnnotations` or an assertion fails in one subtest (e.g., the new 40003-row case), the cleanup never runs and the next subtest's `InsertMulti` with IDs 1..N will fail with a primary-key conflict, producing confusing cascading failures instead of a single clear failure. Registering the cleanup before creating data (or not hardcoding IDs) would make failures isolated.

keycloak-37429.issue: Wrong locale script: The new `totpStep1` value is written in Traditional Chinese (您的手機、應用程式), but this file is the Simplified Chinese (`zh_CN`) locale. Every other line in this file, including the unchanged `totpStep2`/`totpStep3`, uses Simplified Chinese (手机、应用程序). Users of the zh_CN locale will see a mixed-script message. It should be rewritten in Simplified Chinese, e.g. "请在您的手机上安装以下应用程序之一：".

Possible Bug: The new value uses a java.text.MessageFormat choice clause: `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`. This only renders correctly if the message is processed by MessageFormat. Admin console messages in this file are consumed by the admin-ui JS frontend, which performs simple `{n}` placeholder substitution rather than MessageFormat formatting; in that path the raw text `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` would be shown to the user instead of "value"/"values". If this key is only ever formatted server-side via MessageFormat this is fine, but that should be verified for the admin messages bundle specifically.

Unmanaged dependency versions: The newly added dependencies (`owasp-java-html-sanitizer` 20240325.1 and `commons-text` 1.13.0) hardcode their versions directly in this pom instead of using `dependencyManagement` or version properties, which is the usual convention in multi-module projects for keeping versions consistent and upgradable in one place. If the parent pom already manages these artifacts, the explicit versions will silently override that management. Low severity, but worth aligning with the project's dependency-management practice.

Wrong Language: The Lithuanian `totpStep1` message was replaced with Italian text ("Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:"). Lithuanian users of the account theme will see an Italian instruction for setting up an OTP authenticator. This appears to be a copy-paste mistake; it should be the Lithuanian equivalent (e.g., "Įdiekite vieną iš šių programų savo mobiliajame telefone:"), consistent with the other locales in this PR which each received a properly translated version of the same message.

Dangling list reference: The new `loginTotpStep1` text ends with a colon ("Installer en av følgende applikasjoner på mobilen din:" - "Install one of the following applications on your mobile:") but no list of applications follows anywhere in the message. The previous text named FreeOTP and Google Authenticator with links; the replacement now promises a list that the user will never see, unless the login page separately renders an application list for this key. Note also that the English source file (`messages_en.properties`) was not changed for `loginTotpStep1` in this PR, so the Norwegian translation may now diverge from what the English page shows. Verify that the theme actually appends the app list after this message; if not, restore the app names.

MessageFormat compatibility: The changed key now uses Java ChoiceFormat syntax (`{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`) and single-brace placeholders, replacing the previous double-brace form (`{{0}}`). The double-brace form suggests this bundle is consumed by the account console frontend, where placeholders may be escaped/rendered differently than by server-side `MessageFormat`. If the account UI's message formatting does not support ChoiceFormat, the literal text `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` would be shown to users instead of "value(s)". The identical change in the admin-ui and login theme files suggests this is intentional, but it is worth verifying that the account console's rendering path actually evaluates the choice pattern before merging.

Wrong language: The `loginTotpStep1` value in the Lithuanian (`messages_lt.properties`) file was replaced with Italian text ("Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:"). Lithuanian users will see an Italian instruction on the login page. The value should be translated to Lithuanian (e.g., "Įdiekite vieną iš šių programų savo telefone:"), matching the pattern used in the other locale files in this PR.

sentry-80168.issue: Abstract methods not implemented: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` but provides no implementation for its abstract methods (`get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). If this handler is ever instantiated (e.g., via `Detector.detector_handler` in `process_detectors` when a detector of this group type is processed), Python will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ... with abstract methods ...`. Previously the class was concrete (it implemented `evaluate` returning `[]`); the new version silently turns a safe no-op into a runtime crash path. If this group type is not yet registered/used, consider keeping a stub implementation or a guard until the real implementation lands.

Silent duplicate overwrite: The old code explicitly detected duplicate group keys in a detector's results, logged an error ("Duplicate detector state group keys found"), and skipped the duplicate. The new dict-based approach (`results[result.group_key] = result` in `evaluate`, and the dict return type in `process_detectors`) silently overwrites the earlier result with the last one for a duplicated group key. Since the removed comment said "This shouldn't happen - ... we should investigate this", a duplicate now indicates a real bug but is dropped without any log or metric, making the regression invisible. Consider logging an error (or asserting) when a key is already present in the dict.

Possible test bug: In `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe`, the expected occurrence is built via `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, but `expected_result` uses `group_key="group_key"`. Since `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` derives the occurrence fingerprint from the passed group key (`handler.build_fingerprint(group_key)`), the expected occurrence's fingerprint will be for `"val1"` while the actual result produced for group key `"group_key"` will have a different fingerprint. If the assertion compares the occurrence (e.g., via the patched `StatusChangeMessage.__eq__` or direct equality), this mismatch would make the test fail or, worse, silently pass due to a comparator that ignores fingerprints. The occurrence should be built with the same group key used in the expected result.

Inconsistent test data: In `test_state_results_multi_group`, the data packet sets `group_vals` to `{"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}`, but the expected occurrence for `group_2` is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(..., "group_2", 6, ...)`, using value 6 instead of 10. The mock builder currently ignores the `value` argument, so the test passes, but the mismatched value makes the test misleading and will break silently-wrong behavior if `build_occurrence_and_event_data` ever starts using `value`. The expected occurrence should be built with the actual packet value (10).

sentry-80528.issue: Dead code / possible bug: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, a copy of the monitor config is made and `schedule_type` is converted to its human-readable display value on the copy, but the function then returns the original `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the modified `config`. The computed copy is discarded, so the context always contains the raw `schedule_type` integer rather than the display name. If the intent was to show the human-readable schedule type, the return should use `config` instead of `monitor_environment.monitor.config`.

Docstring mismatch: The `get_failure_reason` docstring contains typos ("humam readible") and its third example ("A failed check-in was detected") does not match the actual singular output, which is status-specific (e.g. "An error check-in was detected"). Minor, but worth fixing while the code is being moved.

sentry-95633.issue: This newly-added except block discards the error with a bare `pass` - no logging, no re-raise. If the wrapped call ever fails, the failure is silently swallowed and there's no way to diagnose what went wrong.
sentry-95633.suggestion: Log the exception (e.g. `logger.warning(...)`) or re-raise it instead of silently passing.

sentry-95633.issue: Eager thread spawn: In `__init__`, `FixedQueuePool` is constructed immediately when the factory is created in `thread-queue-parallel` mode, which spawns `max_workers or 20` daemon worker threads at construction time. Unlike the other modes (where the `ThreadPoolExecutor`/`MultiprocessingPool` work is tied to strategy creation), merely instantiating the factory — e.g., for CLI validation or in code paths that never call `create_with_partitions` — now costs 20 live threads. Also note `max_workers or 20` silently substitutes 20 when `max_workers` is None or 0, which differs from the "max workers" semantics of the other parallel modes; consider making the default explicit or validating the value.

Shutdown leaves dangling strategy: `shutdown()` shuts down the pool and sets `self.queue_pool = None`, but any `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` previously returned by `create_with_partitions` still holds a reference to that pool and keeps its commit thread running. If the strategy's `submit()` is invoked after `shutdown()` (e.g., in-flight messages during teardown, as the graceful-shutdown test exercises), `assert self.queue_pool is not None` in `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` has already passed, but the strategy will keep submitting into a shut-down pool whose queues raise `queue.ShutDown`; the resulting exception path marks offsets complete without processing them, so those messages can be committed as done despite never being handled. Consider having the factory coordinate strategy shutdown, or make the strategy resilient to a shut-down pool.

Data loss on processing errors: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, if `result_processor` raises, the exception is logged and the offset is marked complete in the `finally` block. The message is then effectively dropped: `OffsetTracker` will consider it processed and the commit loop will commit past it, so the message is never retried. This silently converts an at-least-once consumer into at-most-once for any transient error (e.g., a DB timeout while handling an uptime result). If the failed item is the highest offset in the partition, the offset is committed on the next commit cycle and the data is permanently lost. Consider leaving the offset outstanding on failure, or routing failures to a retry/dead-letter path.

Failed decodes silently dropped: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the `except Exception` handler marks the failing message's offset as added and completed, so a message that fails to decode or group is skipped and its offset becomes committable. Combined with the commit loop, this means malformed/unexpected payloads are permanently dropped with only a log line. If dropping is intentional for poison messages, it should be explicit (e.g., a dedicated metric/counter and comment); otherwise the offset should not be completed so the message is retried.

Performance: offset scan cost: `get_committable_offsets` iterates `range(start, max_offset + 1)` while holding the partition lock. If a partition has a large gap between `last_committed`/`min_offset` and `max_offset` (e.g., a compacted topic or large offset jump after a seek), this loop runs once per second per partition over potentially millions of offsets, blocking `add_offset`/`complete_offset` for that partition. A sorted structure or heap per partition would avoid the linear scan.

Flaky assertion: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys hash to exactly 3 distinct queue indices. The assignment uses Python's `hash(group_key) % num_queues`, which is not guaranteed to cover all 3 queues for an arbitrary set of 20 keys (and string hashing is randomized per process unless PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed). On some runs only 1 or 2 queues will be hit, making this test intermittently fail. A weaker assertion (e.g., `1 <= len(queue_indices) <= 3`, or checking distribution over many more keys) would be deterministic.

Race condition in test: In `test_stats_reporting`, the assertion `stats["total_items"] > 0` is made immediately after submitting 10 items, but worker threads may have already drained the queues before `get_stats()` is called, making `total_items` 0 and failing the assertion. The test should either block processing until after the stats check or tolerate either value.

Test contradicts implementation: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` asserts that no offsets are committed when processing fails (`len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`). However, in the queue worker implementation, exceptions raised by `result_processor` are caught and logged, and `complete_offset` is still called in the `finally` block. This means offset 100 will be marked complete even though processing failed, and the commit loop will commit offset 102 once offset 101 completes. The test's assertion will therefore fail (or, if it passes, it only passes due to timing — the 1-second commit loop may not fire before the polling window ends), making it flaky and asserting behavior the implementation does not have. The test should either assert that the failed offset is still committed (matching actual behavior) or the implementation should not complete offsets for failed messages.

Resource leak on failure: In each of the new `test_thread_queue_parallel_*` tests, `factory.shutdown()` is called after the `with mock.patch...` block and after assertions. If any assertion inside the block fails (or the polling loop times out), `factory.shutdown()` is never reached, leaving up to `max_workers` daemon worker threads and a commit thread running for the rest of the test session. Using try/finally (or a fixture) around shutdown would prevent leaked threads from affecting other tests.

Private API usage: The Kafka integration test drives the arroyo `StreamProcessor` via private methods `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()`. These are not part of arroyo's public interface and may change without notice, breaking this test on arroyo upgrades. Consider using the public `run()`/`signal_shutdown()` path or a small helper.
